title: Why Is the US-Canada Border Straight? It Actually Isn't
summary: From the Lake of the Woods to the Pacific, the US-Canada border follows the 49th parallel, set in 1818 and extended in 1846. But on the ground it is a chain of straight lines between monuments, one Alberta marker sits about 370 m south of the parallel, and from the Atlantic to the Pacific more than half of the border runs through water.
tags: why is the us canada border straight
sources: Boundary length 8,891 km (5,525 miles) across North America; over 8,000 monuments and reference points; a 6 metre (20 foot) wide clear vista along the land boundary, 3 m (10 ft) on either side of the line (International Boundary Commission, The Boundary): https://internationalboundarycommission.org/en/about/the-boundary.php

Land boundary 5,061 km identified by a series of straight lines which intersect at boundary monuments; 5,528 boundary monuments; 2,172 km of the land boundary runs through forest where the vista must be cleared on a regular basis; Atlantic to Pacific 6,416 km = 2,878 km land + 3,538 km water (3,538 / 6,416 = 55%); Pacific to Arctic (Alaska) 2,475 km (International Boundary Commission, Did you know?): https://internationalboundarycommission.org/en/the-boundary-and-you/interesting-facts.php

Treaty history: 1783 line from the northwesternmost point of Lake of the Woods due west to the Mississippi; 1818 Convention Article II, Lake of the Woods along the 49th parallel to the Stony Mountains (Rockies); 1846 Oregon Treaty westward along the 49th parallel to the Strait of Georgia, then through Juan de Fuca Strait to the Pacific; 1908 treaty for fuller demarcation; 1925 treaty changed the 49th parallel line from a slightly curved line between monuments to a series of straight lines (International Boundary Commission, History): https://internationalboundarycommission.org/en/about/history.php

The 49th parallel east of the Rockies was originally surveyed during the years 1872 to 1875; latitude determined by astronomic observations at about 32-kilometre (20-mile) intervals; the prairie section resurveyed, mapped and monumented 1909-1912 (International Boundary Commission, Section E, Gulf of Georgia to the Northwesternmost Point of Lake of the Woods): https://internationalboundarycommission.org/en/maps-coordinates/maps/section-e.php

Monument 347 (Alberta/Montana): N 48 59 48.0, W 111 34 32.5 (NAD83, averaged grid shift; NAD27 N 48 59 48.04); neighbouring monuments 343-351 used for the drawn chain. 12.0 seconds of latitude south of 49 N at about 30.9 m per second = about 370 m (Map Minutes calculation from the official listing, which is for information only and not the legal definition) (International Boundary Commission, 49th Parallel AB-SK-MB/MT-ND geographical coordinates listing): https://www.internationalboundarycommission.org/uploads/maps/21-49th_parallel_prairies/49th%20parallel%20ab_sk_mb-mt_nd%20(english).pdf

Convention of 1818, Article II: a line drawn from the most North Western Point of the Lake of the Woods along the forty Ninth Parallel of North Latitude ... from the Lake of the Woods to the Stony Mountains; signed London, 20 October 1818 (Avalon Project, Yale Law School): https://avalon.law.yale.edu/19th_century/conv1818.asp

Oregon Treaty, Article I: the line of boundary shall be continued westward along the said forty-ninth parallel of north latitude to the middle of the channel which separates the continent from Vancouver's Island, and thence southerly ... through Fuca's Straits to the Pacific Ocean; signed Washington, 15 June 1846 (Avalon Project, Yale Law School): https://avalon.law.yale.edu/19th_century/br-1846.asp

1818: commissioners fixed the border at the 49th parallel from the Lake of the Woods to the Rocky Mountains; west of the Rockies the decision was postponed; in 1843 jingoists raised the slogan '54 degrees 40 minutes or fight'; Polk proposed the 49 degree line and Britain accepted with modifications that reserved the whole of Vancouver Island; Senate ratified 18 June 1846 (US Department of State, Office of the Historian, Oregon Territory, 1846): https://history.state.gov/milestones/1830-1860/oregon-territory

Treaty of 24 February 1925, Article II: the boundary along the 49th parallel shall be defined as consisting of a series of right or straight lines joining adjacent monuments, replacing the definition under which the line between monuments had the curvature of the parallel (Foreign Relations of the United States 1925, Office of the Historian): https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1925v01/d387

State v. Norman, 145 Wn.2d 578 (Washington Supreme Court, 21 February 2002): 'We hold that this state's northern boundary is coextensive with the international boundary as marked'; the border does not lie on the 49th parallel as currently located; customs sites lay north of the parallel but south of the border; in the 1858-1862 survey the English Commissioner reported errors 'as great as 860 feet and none less than 180 feet' between the Similkameen and the Kettle River when US and British points were linked, attributed to local deflection of the plumb line and resolved by running a mean parallel; the boundary between marks was agreed to be a straight line (FindLaw): https://caselaw.findlaw.com/wa-supreme-court/1329211.html

HistoryLink Essay 5199 (Kit Oldham, 2003): local land masses create gravitational pulls that deflect plumb lines and skewed the latitude readings; marked points were joined by straight lines while a parallel is curved; three defendants charged after searches at border crossings argued their alleged crimes occurred north of the parallel: https://www.historylink.org/File/5199

1783 boundary to run due west from Lake of the Woods to the Mississippi, which rose farther south than shown on the Mitchell map (1755) the description rested on; the 49th parallel (1818) very roughly approximates the northern watershed of the Mississippi-Missouri drainage system of the Louisiana Territory, bought by the US from France in 1803; on the prairies the markers were mounds of sand or grass sod and later iron posts; in forest a vista is cut on each side of the line; the 1783 line ran by the St Croix, the St Lawrence, Lake Ontario, the Niagara, Lake Erie, Lake St Clair, Lake Huron and Lake Superior (The Canadian Encyclopedia, Boundaries): https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/boundaries

The 49th parallel boundary actually consists of several chords drawn between astronomically determined points on the curved parallel; Lake of the Woods to the Rockies agreed in the Convention of 1818, Rockies to the Strait of Georgia by the Oregon Treaty of 1846 (The Canadian Encyclopedia, Forty-ninth Parallel): https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/forty-ninth-parallel

Convention of 1818: Article III left the Oregon Country west of the Rockies free and open to both Britain and the US for 10 years (The Canadian Encyclopedia, Convention of 1818): https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/convention-of-1818

The first instance of a boundary drawn first on paper then traced on the ground; latitude determined with the zenith telescope (Talcott method) (American Society of Civil Engineers, Historic Civil Engineering Landmark: United States-Canadian Boundary Survey): https://www.asce.org/about-civil-engineering/history-and-heritage/historic-landmarks/united-states-canadian-boundary-survey

The Mississippi River begins at Lake Itasca, Itasca State Park, Minnesota (Minnesota Department of Natural Resources, Mississippi River Headwaters): https://www.dnr.state.mn.us/state_parks/itasca/headwaters.html

Map data: Natural Earth (public domain) https://www.naturalearthdata.com and US Census Bureau cartographic boundary files (public domain) https://www.census.gov/geographies/mapping-files/time-series/geo/carto-boundary-file.html

scenes.narration: This border looks like someone drew it with a ruler.
Across the West, it follows one line of latitude: the {49th|forty-ninth} parallel.
So why is the US-Canada border a straight line? And here's the twist: it isn't. Not exactly.
Zoom in on one marker in Alberta, and it sits about {370 m|three hundred and seventy metres} south of that line. And the law sides with the marker.
By the end, you'll know why they chose a line of latitude, how crews marked it, and where the border gives up on straight lines.
It starts in {1783|seventeen eighty-three}. The peace treaty said: from the Lake of the Woods, run due west to the Mississippi.
But the Mississippi rises further south. A line due west never meets it. The treaty's map, from {1755|seventeen fifty-five}, had the river wrong.
So in {1818|eighteen eighteen}, Britain and the US chose something simpler: the {49th|forty-ninth} parallel, from the Lake of the Woods west to the Rockies.
If maps like this are your thing, subscribe. There's a new one every Wednesday.
Why the {49th|forty-ninth}? It very roughly follows the top of the Missouri River's basin: land the US bought in {1803|eighteen-oh-three}, in the Louisiana Purchase.
This line was drawn on paper first, and traced on the ground later. And to find a parallel, you don't need to know the land. Just the stars.
West of the Rockies, Britain and the US shared the Oregon Country. Some Americans wanted the line way up here, at {54°40'|fifty-four forty}.
In {1846|eighteen forty-six}, they settled on the {49th|forty-ninth}, all the way to the Pacific. And Britain kept all of Vancouver Island.
Then someone had to find it on the ground. From {1872|eighteen seventy-two} to {1875|eighteen seventy-five}, crews fixed the latitude by the stars, about every {32 km|thirty-two kilometres}.
On the open prairie, they marked it with mounds of earth and sod, and later with iron posts.
West of the Rockies, when British and American crews compared their marks, some were up to {860 feet|eight hundred and sixty feet} apart.

data.source: State v. Norman (Wash. 2002), citing the 1861 survey

scenes.narration: The culprit: mountains. Their mass tugs on a plumb line and skews a reading of the stars. So the crews split the difference.
And between marks, the line runs straight, while a true parallel curves. In {1925|nineteen twenty-five}, a treaty made it official: straight lines, from monument to monument.
Here's that marker in Alberta: monument {347|three forty-seven}, about {370 m|three hundred and seventy metres} south of the {49th|forty-ninth} parallel.
And the marker wins. In {2002|two thousand two}, Washington's Supreme Court ruled that the state ends at the border as marked, not at the parallel.

data.source: State v. Norman, Washington Supreme Court, 2002

scenes.narration: In the east, the border barely tries to be straight. It follows the {St. Croix|Saint Croix} and {St. Lawrence|Saint Lawrence} rivers, and cuts through four of the Great Lakes.
From the Atlantic to the Pacific, more than half of the line runs through water.

data.title: Mostly *water*
data.source: Intl. Boundary Commission: 3,538 of 6,416 km in water

scenes.narration: All told, the border runs {8,891 km|eight thousand eight hundred and ninety-one kilometres}, Alaska included.
Crews still look after more than {8,000|eight thousand} markers, and clear a strip called the vista, {6 m|six metres} wide, even through forest.
So is the US-Canada border a straight line? From far away, yes. Up close, it's thousands of short straight lines, and it runs wherever the markers stand.
There's a new map every Wednesday. Pick one, and I'll see you there.

data.tagline: The US and Canada, explained on the map
